title: With Due Respect (Vol. 7) -- Ch. 5: Tycoon and Philanthropist
keywords: the heart and soul of SM
primary_topics: Chapter 5 of 'With Due Respect' (Vol. 7) -- CJP's May 17, 2009 Inquirer column profiling taipan Henry Sy Sr. as both 'tycoon and philanthropist,' opening with his economic creed that in a capitalist democracy 'fabulous wealth can be justified only by the zeal to share it with the poor'
The SM Foundation's scholarship program -- the 'heart and soul of SM' -- which had produced 1,176 graduates, as the proof of philanthropy CJP went to the SMX to witness

Sy's business philosophy of 'SYnergy' (sticking to a core, interconnected empire of retail, malls, real estate and banking) and the scale it reached -- three of the world's biggest malls, ~P150 billion in revenues, over 75,000 employees

Sy's personal 'SYmmetry' and 'SYmphony with God' -- a humble, family-centered, faith-anchored life that places 'a house of the Lord' at the center of his projects and now channels his passion from accumulating wealth to distributing it, joining the league of Gates, Ford, Rockefeller and Li Ka Shing
sub_topics: The economic creed: 'in a capitalist democracy such as the Philippines, private enterprise is both the engine of economic growth and the propellant of social responsibility,' so CJP measures a conglomerate 'not so much by the profits it makes but by its ardor in caring for the less fortunate' -- 'fabulous wealth can be justified only by the zeal to share it with the poor'

Passion for philanthropy: he accepted to speak at the '13th Presentation of SM Scholar-Graduates' to see how 'one of the biggest conglomerates' fulfills that duty, and 'was not disappointed' -- the Sy family celebrated it 'as significantly as their annual shareholders' meeting'

The scholarship flagship: the SM Foundation, 'the heart and soul of SM,' runs educational, health and livelihood programs but treats scholarships as its 'flagship' -- then 750 beneficiaries (103 graduating that year, including five magna and 20 cum laude) across 29 institutions, with 1,176 graduates to date, and SM personnel offering them jobs on the spot

A personal arc with the brand: CJP recalls buying shoes 'at the original Shoemart store in Carriedo Street... at... P10 a pair' in the 1950s, marveling as it became SM -- now with 'three of the world's biggest malls' (Megamall, Mall of Asia, North Edsa), 'nearly P150 billion in revenues,' 'over 75,000' employees and '100 stores'

'SYnergy': Sy 'sticks to his core business and area of expertise,' so the seemingly diversified empire is 'really interconnected' -- retail, tourism, shopping centers, real estate and banking -- under his philosophy of 'SYnergy'

'SYmmetry': though hugely successful, Sy 'remains humble, self-effacing, and low profile,' treasuring his children as 'teammates and friends' and his wife Molly as his 'lifetime companion'; his 'God-oriented, family-centered lifestyle' he calls 'balance,' but CJP prefers 'SYmmetry' -- 'harmony and evenhandedness in personal relations' -- noting Sy places 'a house of the Lord' (the Chapel of the Eucharistic Lord; the Shrine of Jesus) at the center of his projects

'SYmphony with God': acclaimed among the world's richest, Sy 'has not forgotten his roots,' recalling he 'was once poor'; his 'passion is no longer to accumulate more wealth but to distribute it to the hopeless and the helpless,' placing him among 'mega philanthropists like Bill Gates, Henry Ford, John Rockefeller, and Li Ka Shing'

Philanthropy as a path to God: 'for the endowed, it is the way to a final reunion with God' -- invoking Matthew 25, that the Lord asks not about 'bank accounts' or 'degrees' but 'whether we shared our resources with the poor' -- a 'SYmphony with God,' proving one can be 'both a tycoon and a philanthropist, an entrepreneur and a Christian, a hard-knuckled realist and a softhearted humanist'

one_paragraph_summary: Chapter 5 of 'With Due Respect' (Vol. 7), CJP's May 17, 2009 Inquirer column, profiles taipan Henry Sy Sr. as both 'tycoon and philanthropist,' opening with his economic creed: 'in a capitalist democracy... private enterprise is both the engine of economic growth and the propellant of social responsibility,' so a conglomerate's success is measured 'not so much by the profits it makes but by its ardor in caring for the less fortunate' -- 'fabulous wealth can be justified only by the zeal to share it with the poor.' Speaking at the 13th Presentation of SM Scholar-Graduates, he found the proof: the SM Foundation, 'the heart and soul of SM,' treats its scholarships (then 750 beneficiaries, 1,176 graduates to date) as its flagship. Recalling that he bought shoes at the original Carriedo Shoemart 'at... P10 a pair' in the 1950s, he marvels at its growth into SM -- 'three of the world's biggest malls,' '~P150 billion in revenues,' 'over 75,000' employees -- under Sy's philosophy of 'SYnergy' (an interconnected core of retail, malls, real estate and banking). Yet Sy 'remains humble... and low profile,' treasuring his wife Molly and children and placing 'a house of the Lord' at the center of his projects -- a life Sy calls 'balance' but CJP renames 'SYmmetry.' Having 'not forgotten his roots,' Sy's 'passion is no longer to accumulate more wealth but to distribute it to the hopeless and the helpless,' joining 'mega philanthropists like Bill Gates... and Li Ka Shing.' For the endowed, CJP concludes, philanthropy is 'the way to a final reunion with God' -- by Matthew 25, the Lord asks 'whether we shared our resources with the poor' -- a 'SYmphony with God' proving one can be at once 'a tycoon and a philanthropist, an entrepreneur and a Christian.'
